canonical_items.text: MODULE – I: CONVERSATION
A note on the expressions to be used on certain occasions

While speaking English — or in the spoken form of English — certain expressions are to be used because the English language is very formal and official. As learners and users of English it is necessary that the formal British idiom is learnt to make official deals, and transactions absolutely formal communicative and clear.

In the course of any conversation it is necessary to use the correct idiom, expression and usage without the influence of the mother tongue or vernacular, which includes manners and etiquette. You are expected to be very formal, and behave courteously with manners in any situation, especially while in group discussions etc.
On meeting a person for the first time in the day the usual greeting is Good morning Sir / Madam / Raju etc.

canonical_items.text: Some times you may have to seek permission from your superiors.
Will you please excuse me sir. May I leave the room sir. May I answer your questions sir. (When it is not your turn)
Gratitude
Thanks is a very vital aspect of British manners. You say,
Thank you, Sir / Madam. That is very kind of you, Raju. I’m really grateful to you sir, for your timely help.
How do you respond to thanks and gratitude expressed. When someone says, “Thank you, Raju” you say,
That’s all right, Sekar. — or — Not at all, Sekar. — or — It’s a pleasure. — or — Don’t mention it. — or — No mention please. — or — You are most welcome.
(Responding to gratitude and thanks is very normal behavior — don’t use Indianisms or coin your own answer, this is the standard form, stick to it if you want to be correct.)

Some common expressions in English

I am thirsty – I am hungry – I am sleepy – I am happy – I am bored – I feel dull – I am excited – I am contented – I am unhappy – I am sad – I am sorry – I am late – I am in time – I am a doctor – I am a lawyer – I am a software engineer.

Framing questions
Framing question in the conservation is a very vital part of communication.
The basic form of a question are direct beginning with question markers viz. What, Where, When, Why, How.
Where do you live? What brings you here? Where is the book? Why are you late? How old are you?

A Question is generally asked for seeking information or classification. It has certain other functions as well. Some of them are as follows:
Inviting — Would you like to attend the party? Request — Could you lend me your book? Offering help — Could I carry your brief case? Permission — May I come in? Suggestion — Could you change the date of the meeting?
Note: The word order is very important in any question. Avoid translating questions from the vernacular.

Clerk: Please go to counter number 14, he will help you.

canonical_items.text: 4. A conversation between a doctor and patient in which the patient complains about a headache

Doctor: Please come in, sit down. What is the matter?
Patient: I’ve an headache right across my forehead.
Doctor: Since when?

Doctor: Is it a continuous pain or a kind of shooting pain at intervals?
Patient: It’s a continuous one.
Doctor: All right. I’ll give you some tablets.
Patient: Could it be due to any defect in my vision?
Doctor: It doesn’t look like. Take these tablets. One tablet each thrice a day.
Patient: Do you think I’ll be alright by tomorrow? I have to go on a long journey tomorrow.
Doctor: You should be.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor.

Manager: Yes, please… please fill in this form. You’ll have to be introduced by someone who has an account here. Then you’ll have to deposit at least a hundred rupees.
Customer: But why an introduction? After all I’m putting my money here.
Manager: That’s true madam. The introduction is in your own interest, otherwise someone else can open an account in your name and you’ll be responsible for the transaction.
Customer: That’s true. Thank you. I’ll bring the form soon along with a cheque for my initial deposit.
Manager: I see. All right. I’ll be back soon. Thank you.
Customer: Thank you, Madam.

Y: Yes, only then they will consider your application.

canonical_items.text: MODULE – II: VOCABULARY
Introduction

Vocabulary is the most vital part of learning a language. As most of the learners in this course are familiar with the basic vocabulary, the areas of confusion is made clear with regards to spelling and usage. Language experts are of the opinion that every profession has its own register of vocabulary. This course aims at helping the learner pass over the intermediary stage before settling down to a profession, which has its own register.

Pronunciation is an essential part of communication of the language. Only standard pronunciation of R.P. – Received Pronunciation helps communicate in English, though there are many dialects in English and the English spoken in different parts of the world have variations and differences.

It is imperative that students in India learn the R.P. which is the standard used by the IELTS of Cambridge while recruiting candidates for higher studies, education and immigration to the countries where English is the official language.

As the duration of this course is limited, attention is drawn towards words which are often mis-spelt, misused or mispronounced. The only sure method of learning pronunciation of English is through the recognized system of phonetic symbols. But as most of the learners in this course are not likely to have knowledge of phonetics, to use such symbols in this course would be futile and pedantic. However, for the present purpose, learning pronunciation from the instructors in the class room is the only practical option available.

English words are dependent on accents — without accents words cannot be pronounced properly. Words are formed by a single speech unit known as “Syllable”. For example, the word “cut” has one speech unit. Based on the syllables, words are classified into different categories.

What is a sentence?

A sentence is a group of words that conveys meaning, with subject and a verb. In other words a group of words which gives a complete sense is called a sentence.
Eg. The country is under the grip of a drought. The Rose is a beautiful flower.
Note: The right arrangement of words is very important otherwise the entire meaning of words is lost or misunderstood. Every Sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

Assertive sentence or Statement — is a sentence which gives us information about something. It can be in the affirmative or it can be Negative.

Interrogative sentence or Question — is a sentence which raises a question to get some information about something. It ends with a question mark. It can also be in the affirmative or negative.

canonical_items.text: Imperative sentence — is a sentence which gives orders, makes requests or gives advice. It ends with a full stop. It may be affirmative and negative.

canonical_items.text: There are six kinds of adjectives.
Adjectives of Quantity — it answers the question “How much?”
He had much money. There is little food in the house. He wants some money. He did not eat any bread. He had sufficient bread. He ate the whole cake.
Adjective of Number — answering the question, “How many?”
All men are mortal. Many women were not there. Several men came to see the line. He had five rupees in his pocket. Some men are rich. The first boy won the prize. Most men are lazy.

Distributive Adjective — which refers to each one of a number:
Each woman carried a basket. Every word of it is true. Either pen will do. Neither boy is likely to pass.
Demonstrative adjectives — answer the question “which?”
This house is mine. That house is yours. I like these flowers. I want those apples. I hate such men. She lives on yonder hill.
Interrogative adjectives — it asks questions.
What colour is your skin? Which house is yours? Whose book is this?
Adjectives of quality — answer the question “what kind?”
Babur was a brave king. It was a cloudy day. He was an honest man. Calcutta is a big city. The rose is a beautiful flower.

Verb is a word which denotes an action. It tells us something about the subject.
Eg. He wrote a letter — wrote is a verb.

canonical_items.text: There are three kinds of verbs: Transitive verb, Intransitive verb, Verb of incomplete predication.
Transitive Verb: It requires an object after it to complete its sense.
I eat an apple. He sees a picture. He makes good toys.
Intransitive Verb: It does not need an object to complete its sense.
The man died. The girl slept. The sun shines. Birds fly in the air. He writes legibly.

Verbs of incomplete predication: There are verbs that do not have complete sense but require some word or words after them for this purpose — they are called verbs of incomplete predication.
Eg. A dog is an animal. She looks pretty. They are fair in their dealings. A thief always lives in fear. She became sad. He seems tired.
Note: Present Participle, Gerund, Past Participle and Infinitive are parts of verb.

TENSES
Tense is a term used in grammar to indicate the time of the action or event.
Present Tense 2. Past Tense 3. Future Tense
Each tense has four forms: Simple, Continuous, Perfect and Perfect Continuous
Simple Present: Used to express
An action which is actually happening now or at the present moment — see, how it rains! Sit down. Get out.
A custom or habit — Cows give milk. I regularly get up by 5 a.m. We play tennis every day. He goes to temple every day.
A general truth — The sun rises in the east.
Present Continuous: Used to express an action going on at the time of speaking. The leaves are falling to the ground. The girls are dancing and singing now.

Present Perfect: Used to express an action that was over in the recent past with reference to the time of speaking. The sun has just set. He has already learnt his lesson. The train has just arrived. The queen has just arrived in time. He has grown tall.
Note: I have lived in Chennai for 5 years (means the speaker is still living in Chennai). I lived in Chennai for 5 years (speaker no longer lives in Chennai).

canonical_items.text: Present Perfect Continuous: Shows an action that began in the past and is continuing up to the present time. I have been working for two hours. I have been ill for three days.
Simple Past: Expressing an action that takes place in the Past. I saw an elephant yesterday. My friend died last year. They left the house a week ago.
Past Continuous: Used to express an action begun and continuing in the Past. We were playing when you came. She was singing when I saw her.

Past Perfect: Used to express an action that had been completed before another was started. The train had left before I arrived. I had finished my work before you came. The rain had stopped before you arrived.

Past Perfect Continuous: When there are two actions in the past — the earlier action has been continuing for some time when the later action took place. He had been watching the TV when I visited him yesterday.
Simple Future: Used to express a future action or an event. I shall go to Chennai tomorrow. He will come here next Sunday.
Future Continuous: Used to express an action continuing at some point in the future time. We shall be singing a song. The girls will be playing football.

Future Perfect: Denotes the action will be completed in the future before another future action takes place. I shall have written my letter before he comes. You will have heard this news already. Nobody will have taken anything from you when you go home this afternoon. I hope you will have washed your face before you come into the room again.

Future Perfect Continuous: An action — whether finished or unfinished, will be in progress for some time. We shall have been playing three hours when you visit here. They will have been making preparation for the marriage for two months.

The hunter killed the tiger – Active Voice. The tiger was killed by the hunter – Passive Voice.

In the first sentence, the subject (hunter) is the doer of the action, that is the subject is active. In the second sentence the subject (tiger) is the sufferer or receiver of the action, that is the subject is not active but passive. In the first sentence the verb ‘killed’ is in active voice. In the second sentence the verb ‘was killed’ is in the passive voice.

Adverbs are used to modify verbs.

Subject of the verb: What she says is quite true. That he is an honest man is quite clear. Why she left is a mystery.

A preposition is a word placed before a noun or pronoun to show what relation the person or thing denoted by the noun stands to something else.
Eg. There is a cow in the field. He is fond of tea.

canonical_items.text: Kinds of prepositions
Simple prepositions: At, by, for, off, in, with, on, out, to, through, from…
Compound prepositions: According, above, about, along, amidst, among, around, behind, beside, between, inside, outside, underneath, within, without.
Phrase prepositions & phrasal verbs: According to, in addition to, in place of, along with, in case of, in regard to, because of, in course of, in spite of, by dint of, in favour of, instead of.
The uses of at and in
At is used for a point of time as — He came here at day break, at sunset etc. At is also used with reference to space, for small towns, villages — I met him at Keeranur. I will see him at school.
In is used for a period of time in which something happens — in the morning, in the month of May, etc. In is also used for big towns, cities, countries — He works in Mumbai. He works in Dubai.

The indefinite article “a/an” is also used:
Idiomatically — a few, a little.
In figurative expressions — few, little.
Before numerical expressions — a lot, a thousand, a dozen.
In expressions of price, speed, ratio — 50 kms an hour, three times a day and Rs.100 a meter.
In exclamations before singular countable nouns — What a hot day! What a pretty baby!
With a noun complement, including names of professions — He is a Teacher. She is a dancer. I am an engineer.

‘The’ is a definite article. It is used:
When we refer to some particular person or thing — a) The house I have just bought is spacious. b) Call the boy wearing the blue shirt.
When a singular noun is used to indicate a class — representative in nature. c) The cow is a useful animal. d) The dog is a faithful animal.
Before rivers, ranges of mountains and group of islands — The Ganges, The Thames, The Himalayas, The British Isles, and The Andamans.
Before the ocean, seas, gulfs, bays — The Indian Ocean, The Red Sea, The Arabian Sea, The Bay of Bengal, and The Persian Gulf.
Before names of some countries, some provinces in India — The USA, The UK, The Deccan and The Punjab.
Before the names of certain well known books — The Bible, The Bagavat Gita, The Kuran.
Before adjectives in the superlative degree — May is the hottest month of the year.
When the double comparative of an adverb is used — The higher you go the colder it becomes.
Before an adjective used as a noun — The poor depend on the rich. The wise don’t like the company of foolish.
Before the names of ships, trains, hotels, theatres, clubs, etc. — The Vaigai express, The Taj Hotel, The Sapphire theatre and The INS Virat.

QUESTION TAGS

A question tag is a short question attached to a statement. The fundamental role of a question tag is to draw attention to the statement or to add to it. Question tags are commonly used in conversations, for emphasis and to evoke the right response from the listener.
Remember
Tag questions are always used in contraction form — aren’t, isn’t, didn’t, won’t etc.
The subject of a tag question is never a noun but a pronoun. Isn’t he? Don’t they? Can we? Am I?

An affirmative statement takes a negative tag and a negative statement is followed by a positive tag. The boy is neat, isn’t he? (Negative tag) The boy is not neat, is he? (Positive tag)

1. CORRUPTION AS HUMAN RIGHTS VIOLATION
By C. Raj Kumar, Courtesy “The Hindu”

Having recognized that corruption affects human rights and the rule of law, it is important for the NHRC to develop the right to corruption-free governance, through a number of rights-based strategies in India. Rights-based approaches to governance are those strategies that rest on the conceptual foundation that social and economic goals do not remain policy objectives, but get transformed into rights that are vested with the citizenry — increasing incentives for public vigilance. In this conception there are “right-bearers” and “duty-holders” — the people will have rights relating to various social and economic goals that were hitherto described as policy objectives. The representatives of the government are vested with the duty of ensuring the protection and promotion of the particular right.
2. MOTHER TERESA
By Naveen Chawla, page: 235

Throughout her life Mother Teresa remained humble, simple and in many senses an ordinary woman. Yet she led one of the most extraordinary lives of the twentieth century. She was not erudite, but her distilled wisdom was as profound as that of any philosopher-saint. She believed in taking one small step at a time, yet she handled several complex activities simultaneously in many parts of the world. She gratefully acknowledged the millions in donations and bequests that made her work possible, but remembered only the ‘sacrifice’ money, like that of the little Calcutta boy who ate no sugar for three days to offer her one rupee that was thus saved. Although she lived and worked in largely Hindu India, she made no attempt at conversion. Conversion, she said, was God’s work, not hers. In reflecting this position, she also astutely conformed to her environment, while at the same time being faithful to Jesus, whom she saw in all those whom she ministered to and encountered.
3. GROOMING INDIA’S RURAL MANAGERS
The Institute of Rural Management, Anand — popularly known as IRMA — has grown to become a towering institution for professional management of rural organizations since it came into being in 1979.

This institution, in the country’s milk capital Anand, Gujarat, was founded at the initiation of the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) with the support of the State and central governments and the Swiss Development Central Co-operation. It has been closely working with co-operatives, NGOs, governments and national and international agencies. IRMA got very high ratings in recent surveys. It holds an enviable reputation in terms of industry interface and international linkages.

Apart from giving research and consultation services for improving the management of rural organizations and programmes, IRMA offers post-graduate and doctoral programmes in rural management. Its Programme in Rural Management (PRM) is one of the best in the country for those aspiring to undertake challenging managerial responsibilities in the rural co-operative sector and development organisations.
4. ARE WOMEN MORE DEPENDENT ON RELATIONSHIPS FOR IDENTITY?
Dr. Alan Loy Mc Ginnis

Most studies show that women have more difficulty establishing their singularity than men. The old stereotype is that men live for their work and women live for love; hence, when a relationship ends, a divorce occurs, or a friendship blows up, it is harder on women than on men.

Does that mean that women are by nature weaker and more dependent? Not at all. It has to do with the fact that most small children spend more time during their early years with their mothers than they do with their fathers.

Nancy Chodorow has done some illuminating work in this area. She points out that a little boy soon realizes that he is not like his mother and that he must differentiate himself from this person. Masculinity is defined by separation. A girl, on the other hand, feels no such need and remains close to her mother. These facts have great consequences for the way we cope when we become adults. Males often grow up being good at independence, but having trouble with closeness. Females often grow up being good at relationship, but having problems with independence.
5. HOW DO YOU REACT TO CONFLICTS? REACTIONS ARE REARED BEHAVIOURS

People react to conflicts differently, some calmly and others with an explosive response. Some people flee from the conflict, and others come back fighting. Some individuals look for ways to negotiate, while others keep pushing to get their own way. Just as conflicts come in many forms, so do our reactions.
